p:
No, the decision to open those seats are driven solely on individual needs and what we’re seeing in terms of students coming through the IEP process. Uhm, and so, a child shows up, we evaluate and we give them the program that they uhm, the evaluation team thinks is needed. Uhm, in terms of due process, we have opened up specialized

programs in specific districts to serve and those are community districts to serve students that otherwise would have taken the Carter route.
Now, you mentioned the district is going to get it, you can send it to us later with the seat breakdown per district.
Of course.
Thank you. Uhm, and the positions that are associated with the additional headcount, those are - can you break that down for us as well?
Yes, teachers, classroom paraprofessionals, transportation paraprofessionals, and IEP paraprofessionals.

And you can also send a breakdown of those too? I do want to give a shoutout to our paraprofessionals. I know there’s at least one here and yeah, uhm you know from my time in the classroom, you know I don’t know where I would personally be and where my kids would be without their paraprofessionals. Uhm, during the pandemic, New York City uh public schools launched a program called Sensory Exploration Education and Discovery SEED, providing afterschool and weekend programs

where students with intensive sensory needs can get help from occupational and physical therapists, along with the family educa- engagement component. After the federal COVID-19 stimulus funds expired two years ago, public schools got a grant from the State Education Department. That grant runs out this year. Uh, 94 percent of families agree that the SEED program has been beneficial in addressing their child's sensory needs. That’s a good grade, that’s an A. What is - so that funding is running out from the state, what is the current budget for this program and how many SEED sites does this support?
Currently uhm, 77 seat sites are up and running, fully operational and it costs us about $6 million annually to run that program for nearly 2,000 students.
Okay, so you said 2,000 students are currently utilizing the program?
Uhm, it’s - I don’t want to give the exact number because it’s rolling enrollment but typically between 1,700 and 2,000.

Okay uhm and what resources does the Department of Education need to

ensure you can continue the SEED program including the after school and weekend SEED programs?
We are working on that number. I have to get back to you.

And you know going back to the same questions about mayoral control. Similar - same questions about the caps. Uhm, what advocacy has the department of education done with the state to advocate for continuing this funding?

Well, you know earlier we talked about and I need to apologize for mispeaking. Earlier I quoted Fair Student Funding. What I meant was our funding weights that we - the Chancellor uhm - Fair Student Funding does take into account the localized needs of students. So, I - I was actually talking about the advocacy the Chancellor did at the State Budget hearing around added weights for students with disabilities. Of course when we - if we look at added weights, we’re able to look beyond you know the mandated needs and into spaces such as this.
So, the advocacy centers on the increased uhm, formula for students disabilities, that’s what the advocacy right?
I think that’s - I think that’s one form of it.
Are there other forms?

You know, we’re certainly - I just, I don’t want to say that that’s the only thing that would help. You know we are open to any sort of additional funding that would support this program because of its monumental uh, impact that it’s had on students.

Okay uhm, so just sort of uh, for these particular programs, I’m just trying to make clear, is the DOE going up and saying this program needs $6 million as you just testified, this other program needs whatever the dollars. Are you going up programming by programming, program by program and advocating for the dollar amount in addition to the advocacy you’ve already done around the uhm, the formula uh to increase the funding for students disabilities?
Yeah, so I think you know in general uh, we have conversations about a lot of different uhm topics and certainly when we’re in conversations with CTR and OMB a lot of many specific programs come up.
Thank you. Uhm, and have you spoken to OMB about continuing this funding, this program with city dollars?
Uhm, so yes, we have spoken to OMB about this particular program.

Great, thank you. I want to go back to District 75 for - just for a minute, just to better understand a little bit. You’re saying there are new uh 173 new classes uhm and new seats for District 75. Are we talking new schools that are opening up? Are we talking about putting more seats in existing schools? What’s the mix?
We opened, we put a new District 75 school online uhm this year and then it also includes opening up additional classes in existing schools.
Okay, so you’re mostly talking about expanding existing D75 programs.
Correct.

Okay and is - what has the feedback been on that? Is that what principals or teachers are saying? Like, it makes sense to expand existing programs or do you hear more that we need

new uh schools, new programs in throughout the city? What are you hearing?

We, we hear both but ultimately Chair we are looking at high quality program Close to Home and the vision here is to give as many kids as possible access to programs that are in their geographic district and ideally where their siblings go to school and that’s why we’ve been focusing. You know certainly District 75 play such a vital role. Given the demand and the increases we’re seeing of students with disabilities and the level of need, uhm, District 75 has been what we have been - our go to around uh serving students. Ideally though we are going to be moving and that’s what we have seen in our pilots into that more localized placement of students with the support and that’s why we keep pushing for our specialized programs. It’s the most effective way to do that.

Yeah and I’ll just add a couple things. One, just a reminder that District 75 has grown over 2,800 students since 2020 and this is in contrast to the rest of the city that’s losing enrollment right and I think when it comes to citing a District 75, what I’ve heard from principals, uhm

around the city is this opportunity for inclusion, is something that’s really important to us. So, the site within a school uhm you know allows us to, to, to really promote being inclusive.

Thank you and I do - I don’t think I said it outloud, you know I do appreciate every time you say it, that when you talk about integration, you are also talking about integration of students with disabilities, which is huge. It’s something I think we don’t talk enough about and I’m grateful that you are speaking, using that language, so thank you.
Thank you.

I want to move over to Early Childhood. Uhm, unfortunately the Chair is stuck and so, I’ll be asking some questions on her behalf. Uhm, but here we go. Are you ready? Pull up those documents. She looks ready, okay. 2K pilot, okay, Preliminary Plan includes $73 million in Fiscal 2027 in state funding to begin a 2K pilot next year. The city recently announced that 5 school districts, 6, 10, 18, 23, and 27 will receive new 2K seats next fall. How many extended day and school

day seats will be offered under the 2K program in the first year?

Thank you for that question Chair. Uhm, I’m going to provide something that’s probably not going to be uh satisfying. We are still working through those details. And so, as I mentioned earlier, we released an RFI. That process is still ongoing. We also released two surveys to existing providers. And so, we’re working through those details now to determine the program model and also specific locations and seat counts.
Well, I’ll tell you, I have mixed feelings about that answer.
I’m sorry.
I appreciate that it was an answer. You answered the question honestly, so thank you. Uhm, when - is there a timeline on when you’ll have answers to that question?
So, we have to confirm the timeline but what I can commit to is once we do finalize the information, we are happy to share it with the Council so you can have the information.

Yeah, I think all of us have our constituents stop me in the street asking

this question. Uh, and you know they are very eager. We are all eager in the Council to know when this will be implemented. When they’ll have those details.

And Chair, I will say those who apply to the RFI, those not in the priority districts for the upcoming fall were notified. Those moving to the second phase of the RFI were notified. And so, any of your constituents are aware where they are in the process.
Thank you. I meant the parents.
Oh.

Yeah, I meant the parents. Uhm, the funding for 2K, it jumps to $4 to $25 million in Fiscal 2028 as part of the governor’s commitment however, there’s no baseline funding for 2K. Uhm, what is the DOEs long term funding plan for this population?

I think as we are having conversations about the overall state of uhm our portfolio of early care in education, we are having conversations with the Administration, the Mayor’s

Office and OMB about what that figure could look like and should look like.

Under the Council's Infant and Toddler pilot, the competitive seat rate costs uhm of $40,000. Given the amount of state funding allocated for 2,000 seats, this would not cover the reimbursement rate. Can you confirm?
So, the birth to two pilot includes infants and toddlers.
Uhm, hmm.

Not just two year olds, those 24 months to 36 months. We are looking at what the rate could be for 2K and I would like to remind the Council and folks that the birth to two pilot only included community based organizations. 2K will also include family child care providers.
What is your target rate for the 2K seats and do you believe it’s a competitive rate?
We’re finalizing that now but I would like to think it is a competitive rate.

Okay, I -I - uh, smaller providers have expressed concerns about getting contracts when competing with larger corporate

providers. How is the DOE working to ensure equity when awarding contracts?

So, it’s just what I mentioned earlier around you know we talk about ecosystems and ecosystems include independent care. It includes informal child care. It includes homebased, centerbased care, district school care because if it’s really around parent choice, parents choose different settings for their littles. And so, what we did was we looked at the entire uh permitted license regulated footprint in New York City, which includes regulated care from OCFS, New York State OCFS as well as DOHMH. That also includes our independent program - I mean, uhm, excuse me, our district school programs. And so, looking at where placement currently is, we want to do this on a very thoughtful and measured way. We understand that there is need for 2K. There’s a need for 3K. There’s a need for infant care but that care also exists outside of New York City Public Schools and so we want to be thoughtful about where we place seats. And so, the Mayor’s Office of Child Care and Early Child Education working with us, ACS, talking about interagency

partners, looking at a bunch of data and making sure we overlay that when we are determining seat placement is how we approach this.
I will note that there are some high schools where they need day care, child care for the student population.
That’s the Life Program, correct.

Yes, yes, so I’d love - we’re going to talk offline about that, one of the schools in my district you’re familiar with. Uhm, but I - you know we talk in - here in these meetings, very kind of high level and you look at it as spreadsheets. You need to, you’re running something but there’s also the reality and it was sort of referred to, referenced before about DOE programs versus the community based providers and there are different challenges there. And I’m going to ask two things in how you’re addressing these. One is you are doing a reimbursement rate per child for your community based organizations correct?
That’s correct.

And so, so how do you manage, how do you work with a CBO where you’ve told

them you have whatever 20 seats? You have - you know you gave them funding for 20 seats, only 18 kids, or 17 kids for whatever reason stay in the program and you’ve just taken away, uh, funding for three students but they still have to open the classrooms for those 20 kids. They still have to hire the teachers. They have to do all that contractual work. How do you manage that and still support CBOs with such a rigid structure, given the realities of what the CBOs are facing.

Yeah, I want to acknowledge that. You know I cut my teeth at a community based organization many years ago and so - although I love all of our settings, they hold a special place in my heart. So, I want to leave with that truth. Uhm, we have a base plus model in which our community based organizations are funded and so, they are reimbursed usually on a month lag. Uhm, and it is above their actual enrollment and to your point Chair, it recognizes that there are some costs that are just fixed. And so, you need a teacher for 3 kids, you need a teacher for 15 kids.
You got it.

And so, we are looking at models as we kind of shift into a larger procurement about how we can better reflect those fixed costs but right now in the current contract structure, which has been in, in, in uh, active for about five years now. It does recognize above your actual enrollment for that very reason.

Okay, yeah, I still think there’s some - there are some problems there. Uhm, and it’s clear that there are problems which is why you’re going back and looking at it because you’re aware of them. And you are I assume in conversations with the CBOs, with the ones who provide -
Absolutely.

Second, thank you - second question about that, uh, and it was mentioned again, CBOs versus DOE schools is pay disparity, right? And it is uhm, I know we have a bill in the Council by Chair Lee to address that. Uhm, but that’s uh, you know it’s a really tough call to make. You know so many people at CBOs, they stay because they love their kids and they love the program. And then they go home and they’re met with this - the wait of affordability in New York City. They’re met with the

weight of asking themselves if they are making the right decision for their lives knowing that they can make more at the DOE then they can at the place that they love. How is the DOE addressing the pay disparities between the CBOs and the DOE schools?

First, I want to say there’s no versus, right. That’s not how we operate and for early care in education, we would not be successful without our CBOs. They comprise about 60 percent of our seat capacity and so, there’s no versus. Uhm, we want to also acknowledge that there is pay disparity across the settings and that’s something we are committed to fixing with the Administration. Clearly, the Administration is leading that effort but we have to do that in constant with our labor partners. And so, we are having those conversations but you know, we have - you have our commitment to making sure that our CBO partners are homebased providers are seen in this space because they are very much valued in this work.
I mean is the DOE looking - are New York City Public Schools looking to match the CBO pay scale with that -
That’s not something we can independently decide. That’s something we have to do with our labor partners.
In the past, you provided I guess they’re bonuses. I don’t know what the proper term is.
Many moons ago, there were retention and recruitment bonuses to incentivize folks to come into the field. That’s different, I think that was around $2,500 to $3,500.
During COVID I believe and I believe it was very successful and the teachers are very happy about that, right?

Right, there was also this effort to increase non-union wages to align with DC 37 wages. Again, that’s different from what you know district school teachers under UFT has provided. So, we are having all of those conversations.

Right but there were I guess recruitment retention bonuses for the non-UFT members. The non-DOE schools. I’m talking specifically about CBOs, that they received - the teachers got additional funds, right?
I would have to verify if it was a contingent upon a union affiliation. That happened many years ago but that’s something my team could look into around the recruitment and retention bonuses.

Yeah, because that seemed to have been successful and we want to repeat models that have been successful paying, early child providers, what they deserve right, taking care of as you say, our littles, our babies, which is language I love.

Yeah, I would say you know a bonus and incentive bonus is always welcomed. I think what I’m hearing you say is something that is kind of at the undergirding of what they do to be compensated at a rate that they deserve. And so, a one time payment of $2,500 I’m sure is nice but I’m sure that our educators want a livable wage, a higher wage that’s more aligned with what their colleagues are doing.
They, they deserve it.
Exactly.

They deserve it and I hear the phrase often labor of love and like that’s nice

but that doesn’t pay the rent, you know. Uhm, so and it’s so hard to keep relying on simply the fact people love their job and love their kids. Uhm, you know it isn’t right so I want to move to Head Start, Head Start transitional contracts. The DOE recently transitioned from federally funded Head Start seats to city funded transitional contracts for Head Start delegates. We would like to discuss updates on this process and the future of DOE run Head Start programming. What is the current breakdown of city funded headstart and early headstart seats by school district?
We have that data ready and we can share that after the hearing Chair.
Thank you. Uhm, same question, was the current enrollment in these seats by Head Start and Early Head Start and what is the overall utilization rate and the utilization rate by seat type?
We can share that. I just want to clarify we no longer stratify by Early Head Start and Head Start because those are titles that no longer exist. They’re no longer Head Start programs.
Thank you for the clarification. And how will these seats eventually be integrated into the DOE, Early Childhood ECE system?
I love that question. We’re looking at that now as we think about the overall procurement that will be happening perspectively.
But same day - is there a timeline? Like have you set goals for yourself for integrating that into the DOE?

So, internally yes. So, we can’t give any information proactively about a future procurement because that can create some unintended advantage for folks who are listening to this hearing in that instance. So, yes, we are planning forward for that but we can’t share details on a specific timeline for which that will be released.
You can’t share a timeline of what your goal is for integrating the seats because it’s related to an RFP?
Correct.
Okay, as a now city funded program, what’s the goal for Head Starts, Head Start seats?
Sorry, I don’t think I understand the question.
Well, uhm, the total number of seats for Head Start. What is your goal?

So, we don’t have a goal necessarily. So, one thing that we did when we transitioned from Head Start contracts including Early Head Start to transitional was give the providers an opportunity to convert their seat types. And so, what you’ll see in the data and I’m sure what you saw in the PMMR is that there was a transition of - or actually an increase in infant and toddler seats and a decrease in PreK and 3K seats for the Head Start transitional. So, there’s no goal but we do have a total uh, uhm, portfolio of care that we’ve been trying to maintain for - with the Head Start Program.
And do they have immigration status requirements, these seats?
No, they do not.
So, anyone is eligible for these seats?

So, what we’ve been asking the providers to do was prioritize those families who would normally be eligible for Early Head Start or Head Start, which has categorical eligibility requirements. It does not consider immigration but since these are now CTL funded, they can expand eligibility to include those that are just age eligible and live in the five boroughs.
Thank you. Uh, in the -
I’m ready.
I can tell, you’re ready.
I’m locked in.

I almost want to go to someone else, give you a breath. Uh, uhm, the Fiscal 2026 Budget deal, the Council secured $10 million in funding for the first non means tested infant and toddler seats, also known as birth to two initiative. I first want to thank you for working with the Council to launch this pilot program especially in such a short timeline. How many childcare programs are participating in the pilot program to offer these seats and how are they selected?

Yeah, so originally it was 18 for 240 seats. Right now, we are down to 13 at 170 seats. And what we found was starting mid-year, we ran into issues with staffing, identifying staff to work and start in the program in January but also families often locked in their care starting earlier in the school year, so that September. So, some of our participating providers ran into issues recruiting families specifically for the 24 months to 36 months range. Right now, we’re 88 percent enrolled and what we did was we looked in communities again, taking that overlay of existing care and saying, who has uhm for instance vouchers. We don’t want to have families or providers, excuse me supplant care. We wanted this to be in addition to. And so, also, we looked at existing contracts. Again, a very concentrated timeline to set these up. So, wanting to leverage existing mechanisms to do so. And then looking at the economic need index in communities to determine what- you know meeting the kind of families with the most need.
And so what -
That is kind of the high, highline sorry.
What insights have you gained from this experience that’s going to shape the rollout or the continuation of this and the rollout of the 2K pilot?

Yeah, I think the timing is something we are still evaluating. That January start did not work at our advantage to be honest. I’m mentioning again the staffing and families but what we’ve been doing now in addition to getting the word out about 2K earlier on, we are creating a centralized admissions process for 2K which will help families really direct them into care once they are announced. Really focusing our marketing but also supporting the participating providers no matter the setting on staffing up properly. So, having a bit more runway will allow a lot more success for 2K.

Now, you’re talking about enrollment. You’re talking about managing the Early Childhood System. In the past, there were walls between these two systems where my Early Childhood providers you know they would complain they lost kids but they had no

way to access the - uh, let’s say a waitlist or other kids to fill up those seats and when asked in the past - when I asked in the past about this, to the Early Childhood, uhm, uh of the DOE, the response was very nicely but the response was, well, that’s a different unit. That’s a different division. So, what has been done in the past year or two years to break down those walls to ensure that enrollment is directly related to the work that you’re doing?

Yeah, so what I would like to say and it’s something to kind of your prior point about frankly funding vacant seats is recruitment is everyone’s responsibility. Not just that of New York City Public Schools. It doesn’t just live in my schools. It is everyone’s responsibility. And when I used to work at a community based organization, what makes that role so powerful is that they have an intimate awareness of that community. I would go into the WIC center, right? We would have folks going into the barber shop of the local bodega. You have to know your community and where to find families. Frankly, stand outside of the hospital. You know a baby is born every day. Uhm, but what we

have done around my schools integration and to your point Chair, it is not just the responsibility of the Office of School Enrollment. We are trying to improve that process, make sure that providers and families know how to actually access it. Use it, extend the languages in which it is offered and actually be in community to help families enroll in real time and we’ve worked with the Mayor’s Office on that.

So, I understand all hands on deck but I just want to be clear in my question that, that the offices at the DOE central are working together, that they’re not in silos and what that - and what that communication looks like because in the past, in the past five years since I’ve been on the Council, it has been people in silos and where uhm, the Early Childhood organizations wanted to get more kids but they had to go through three different offices just to figure that out. So, what is communication with the Office of Enrollment for you look like?

So, we actually have weekly meetings with them. And not that meetings is a solution but it’s definitely a tool to make sure that

we are communicating. I would be remiss if I didn’t shout out DIIT, which is a huge part of making sure that My School is operable and so, in addition to meeting with them weekly, we’re meeting with them weekly to talk about the 2K centralized system to iterate on existing systems and then we also beyond the Office of Student Enrollment, which is the primary manager of My Schools, we actually have standing meetings agencywide with reps from different divisions to make sure that we are operating strongly interagencywide.

Just a general point that you’re making about the silos that exist within the Department of Education, I think or NYC Public Schools, uhm, that was desperate in which I entered the reorganization moves that we recently made, which is why so many of the uhm, the pieces that - or structures that support schools are now with the First Deputy Chancellor along with superintendents and our supervising superintendents and I think you know just the way our cabinet operates uh, lends itself to seamless communication between uhm, the Office of Enrollment and uhm our Early Childhood division and I think that’s - that’s one of the

things that I’m super committed to open in the next number of years to make sure that we’re breaking down the silos in NYC Public Schools.

Yeah, I noticed that when I asked one of my questions you gave this face, like shaking your head, like how could anyone think that or do that but the reality is, it’s - you can ask any Council Member it’s happened in the past. It happens with our city agencies. People don’t talk to one another. I appreciate your commitment to this. However, in a $38 billion agency uh, you know things sometimes - that is the reality of it. Uhm, and so, I appreciate your awareness of this and knowing that this Committee is ready to work with you to make sure those silos are broken down, that all of the agencies are talking to each other because it’s for the benefit of our kids and the people who educate our littles, our babies.
New York’s cutest.
Maybe not the middle schoolers but -
The littlest are the cutest yeah.

Yeah, my kids are getting to that age. Speaking of uhm well, and for all kids,

we all deserve safety. Uhm, you know you mentioned it in your DC Hawkins, you are relieved. You are okay. You did great. Uhm, Chancellor I know you said this both publicly, privately, that safety, huge concern. Uhm, we know that there are many facets to the safety of a child. I want to focus right now on school safety officers. The plan includes increased costs for school safety but the additional funding does not increase headcount for these positions. What’s the current budgeted headcount for school safety officers and how many positions are currently filled?

Yeah, thank you for - I know, you know I see my Chief of Safety Mark Rampersant is already at the table and I’m excited to kind of hand it over to him but just to really point out that safety in a school as you know Chair is really centered on relationships and you know it’s never with anyone individual. And so, we’ve been doing a lot of work around ensuring that communication in schools are really strong and uhm, I’m excited to - to kind of continue to think about that with our principals and our school staff but as you know, we don’t also - we also are not uhm, the headcount for

school safety agency - school safety agents doesn’t fall on the DOE. And so, I’ll shift it to Mark so that Mark can address some of these concerns but remember to introduce yourself and for the record.
You’re good, maybe we should just switch.
No thanks. I’m good.
Agreed by the way.

It’s too early to switch. My name is Mark Rampersant, Chief of Safety and Prevention Partnerships and as the Chancellor just mentioned, the NYPD School Safety falls within the scope of the NYPD. So, we don’t directly control their hiring, training or deployment of school safety agents. However, we partner with them on a daily basis to ensure that our schools are safe. They are viable members of our school community and do a great job in supporting, supporting our students. Uhm, currently, the School Safety headcount allotment is 4,015 school safety agents. We are experiencing a massive shortfall as it relates to the School Safety Agents deployed through our school with their current headcount at 3,578. Some of what they’ve done to support the shortfall of school safety

agents,especially in our elementary schools that only have one school safety agent, is the assistant school safety agent program that you probably heard of where 114 school safety agents have been hired and deployed to supplement the single school safety agent at our elementary schools.
Does the 3,578 include those 114 assistant uh school safety officers?
Unfortunately it does.
And talk about some of the issues that uh that you’re facing or the NYPD is facing in terms of hiring school safety agents.

Yeah, so in our daily conversation with School Safety division, some of the things that they were hearing is the prevailing wage. The School Safety agent incoming wage is really low. And so, it is very difficult for them to get takers, or at least young people who are willing to remain with the job, as there are so many other uhm, competing agencies. You know when you were a school safety agent, you’d rather work in a correctional facility than a school, right? That’s really telling right? And so, they are competing with agencies such

as the Corrections Department and their own police department to boot.
And what are some of the strategies? So, it sounds like you’re saying they should be paid more.
I am saying that the current wage is what is challenging for the school safety division to keep their current allotment of school safety agents.
It’s the same thing, same thing.
It is - you said it, not me.

We both said it. We both said it. Beyond the wages, uhm what other recruitment strategies is the DOE engaged in and you know just for color for people who may not be aware that we have principals in my district. Principals throughout the city who want to do after school programs, want to do programs on the weekend for their kids, especially high risk students or in communities that are of higher rates of violence or crime and they are unable to do the programs that we know work for engaging kids. The programs we know make our kids safe because the school safety agents

are not available. Like, that is how important. It is important. It is about keeping our kids safe and making sure we are expanding the programming available to them, so they can continue to be safe and engage in safe activities. So, what recruitment efforts are being made to hire up the number of school safety agents that we need to at least 4,015.

Sure, sure so first of all, thank you very much for that. First and foremost if there’s any principal in our system that’s having a problem with staffing, school, after hours and on weekends, please let me know of that right because that is not a shortfall for us in terms of SSAs, as many of our schools are closed during the weekend. So, the SSAs are in fact available in that respect. Some of the recruitment efforts are exactly what I just shared. They are going to local high schools and even advertising for the school safety, assistant school safety agent program with the hopes of getting recent high school graduates to join the force right? So, 18 years old to 20 years old, that’s the assistant SSA program. So, that’s one of the recruitment

efforts. The other is, advertising the role of the school safety exam at many of our PTA meetings, working with our parent coordinators to get the word out in various different ways by which they get to have face time with families and other bodies.

Let’s go back to evaluation of schools because this is for me like the number one thing. A superintendent goes into a school, let’s say high school as you’re talking about, go into a school. Some of the quantitative markers, test scores, attendance, credit accrual, important things and number of students attending college. Is that last one correct - that they’re looking at the number of students who get into a college? Are they also looking and measuring the number of students for example, that take the civil service exam? Are they looking at measuring the number of students that uhm, that get gainful employment after high school, rather than go to college?
